documentNotes.title: Instructions
documentNotes.statement:
4 Questions, 60 Minutes

Show all work, as partial credit may be earned.

Communicate!  The grader will not attempt to read your mind.

A hand-held calculator may be used.  Its memory must be cleared of data and programs. Calculators may not be shared.

Possibly useful approximations:

$$(1 + x)^n \approx 1 + nx \quad \text{for } |x| \ll 1$$

$$\cos\theta \approx 1 - \theta^2/2! \quad \text{for } \theta \ll 1$$

$$\sin\theta \approx \theta \quad \text{for } \theta \ll 1$$

transcription.notes: Problems document is a clean digital export (text layer good); the solutions document is a low-resolution scan with no text layer. Page 1 of the problems is the cover with instructions (kept in paper.documentNotes); problems 1-4 are on pages 2-5 ('Page 1 of 4' … 'Page 4 of 4'). Points are printed per part as '(a, 8)'; each problem totals 20 (no paper total printed). In the scanned solutions many thin minus signs and negative exponents have faded almost completely (e.g. 'a = (F_o/Nm) − μg', 'T = (N−n)m[μg + (F_o/Nm) − μg]', 'mg sinθ − μN', 'with the − root', '(1+Γ)^{-1}', '(1+Γ)^{-1/2}', '10^{-11}', '(…m/s)^{-2}', '(…m)^{-1}', '10^{-7}', '10^{-4}'); they were read from the faint traces and the surrounding algebra. Printed errors kept verbatim: solution 1(b) 'applied the the entire N-block system' (duplicated word); solution 2(a) prints 'N = μmg cos θ' for the normal force (the next line uses N = mg cos θ); solution 2(b) 'which in inside the house' ('in' for 'is'); problem 2(a) 'on the roof a house' (missing 'of'). Problem 3 names the mass M, while the official solution writes m. Problem 1 prints the force as F_o in the text and F0 in the figure. The solutions page 1 carries a faint handwritten note at the top (illegible, not transcribed). Answers are taken from the official solutions.

problems.statement: A collection of $N$ identical blocks, each of mass $m$, are connected by unstretchable ropes of negligible mass.  The blocks are on a horizontal surface.  An external force $F_o$ acts on Block 1, pulling horizontally to the right.  What is the tension in the rope connecting Block $n$ to Block $n+1$, if:

figures.alt: A row of blocks on a horizontal surface, labelled from left to right N, N-1, …, n+1, n, …, 2, 1, joined by ropes (with dashes marking omitted blocks); an arrow F0 pulls block 1 to the right.

parts.label: (a)
parts.statement: There is no friction between the blocks and the surface?

parts.label: (b)
parts.statement: The coefficient of kinetic friction between each block and the surface is $\mu_k$?  ($F_o$ is large enough to accelerate the blocks despite the friction.)

solution.statement:
**(a, 8)**

The force $F_o$ must accelerate $N$ blocks each of mass $m$:
$F_o = Nma$, so that $a = F_o/Nm$. (4)

Let $T$ be the tension dragging $N$-$n$ blocks to the right.  $F = ma$ gives
$T = (N-n)ma$ (2)

Using $a$,
$T = (N-n)\,F_o/N = F_o\,(1 - n/N)$. (2)

**(b, 12)**

Each block has exerted on it the friction force $\mu mg$. (2)

$F = ma$ applied the the entire $N$-block system gives
$F_o - N\mu mg = Nma$ (2)

Solving for acceleration,
$a = (F_o/Nm) - \mu g$ (2)

Let $T$ be the tension dragging $N$-$n$ blocks to the right.  $F=ma$ gives
$T - (N-n)\mu mg = (N-n)ma$ (2)

so that upon substituting for $a$,
$T = (N-n)m\,[\mu g + (F_o/Nm) - \mu g\,]$ (2)

which gives the final answer,
$T = F_o(1 - n/N)$, the same as without friction. (2)

figures.alt: A roof inclined at 30° to the horizontal (dotted horizontal line) with a box (blue rectangle) near its top; a dimension arrow L runs along the roof from the box to the roof edge. From the edge a vertical house wall drops 3.0 m (vertical arrow labelled 3.0 m) to the ground, where a flower bed 2.0 m wide (arrow labelled 2.0 m) extends from the wall.

parts.label: (a)
parts.statement: A box of nails begins sliding from rest on the roof a house.  The roof makes an angle of 30° above the horizontal.  The coefficient of sliding friction is $\mu_k$ = ¼.  The box slides off the edge of the roof with a speed of 3.5 m/s.  What is the distance $L$ the box slides on the roof before falling off?  Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$  (which also =  9.8 N/kg).

parts.label: (b)
parts.statement: The flower bed extends from the side of the house and is 2.0 m wide.  The edge of the roof is 3.0 m above the ground.  Does the box of nails land in the flowers?  Justify your answer with a calculation that shows where the box lands.  Neglect air resistance.

answer.value: Yes, the box lands in the flowers ($x = 1.9$ m).

solution.statement:
**(a, 10)** Work energy theorem:  $W = \Delta K$ (2)

Setting up the work energy theorem,
$[\,mg\sin\theta - \mu N\,]L = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - 0$, (4)

where $N$ is the normal force.  But from $F = ma$ normal to the roof, $N = \mu mg\cos\theta$ (2)

thus,  $L = \tfrac{1}{2}v^2 / [g\,(\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta)]$
and numerically,
$L = \tfrac{1}{2}(3.5\ \mathrm{m/s})^2 / [(9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2})\,(\sin 30^{\circ} - \tfrac{1}{4}\cos 30^{\circ})\,] = 2.2\ \mathrm{m}$. (2)

(-1 for incorrect units; -1 for gross neglect of significant figures)

Alternative method:
$F = ma$ tangent to the roof gives $a = g\sin\theta - \mu N$ [4]
$= g\sin\theta - \mu g\cos\theta$ [2]
$= 2.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. [1]

Using $v^2 - v_o^2 = 2a(x - x_o)$ [2]

leads to $L = v^2 / 2a = 2.2$ m. [1]

**(b, 10)** Projectile problem:
$v_{oy} = (3.5\ \mathrm{m/s})\sin 30^{\circ} = 1.75\ \mathrm{m/s}$, (1)
$v_{ox} = (3.5\ \mathrm{m/s})\cos 30^{\circ} = 3.03\ \mathrm{m/s} \approx 3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. (1)

For the $x$-direction,
$x = v_{ox}\,t$, (2)

For the $y$-direction (taking down positive)
$y = v_{oy}\,t + \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. (2)

Solve the equations simultaneously by some appropriate strategy.  For instance, eliminating $t$ in the $y$-equation by using the $x$-equation:  $y = v_{oy}\,(x/v_{ox}) + \tfrac{1}{2}g(x/v_{ox})^2$ (2)

Putting in numerical values, solving the quadratic equation correctly, choosing the + root in the quadratic formula (with the − root one gets an $x \lt 0$, which in *inside* the house), one finds $x = 1.9$ m. (2)
Yes, the box lands in the flowers.

problems.statement: A basketball of mass $M$, radius $R$, and moment of inertia $I$ about its center of mass (CM) is set spinning with angular velocity $\omega_o$ about a horizontal axis through its CM.  The CM is originally at rest and located at the height $h$ above the floor.  The basketball is dropped while spinning, and subsequently collides with the floor. Neglect air resistance.

figures.alt: A circle (the basketball) with a curved arrow labelled ω0 showing its clockwise spin; a dotted horizontal line from its centre and a vertical arrow h down to the floor line; a dotted vertical line from the centre to the floor marked x = 0.

parts.label: (a)
parts.statement: Let $K_1$ be the basketball’s kinetic energy just before it collides with the floor.  Write $K_1$ in terms of the given parameters and any needed constants.

parts.label: (b)
parts.statement: Immediately after the first bounce, the basketball is no longer spinning, and its kinetic energy is $\beta K_1$, where $\beta \lt 1$ is a known factor.  What are the horizontal and vertical components of the basketball's velocity immediately after the first bounce?

solution.statement:
**(a, 3)**
By conservation of energy,
$\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega_o^2 + mgh = K_1 + mgR$
so that
$K_1 = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega_o^2 + mg(h - R)$ (3)

**(b, 17)**

Let $(v_x, v_y)$ = velocity of the ball immediately *after* the collision is over.
Given:
$\beta K_1 = \tfrac{1}{2}m(v_x^2 + v_y^2)$ (2)
Since $\beta$ and $K_1$ are known, if either of $v_x$ or $v_y$ is known then so is the other.  Let us find $v_x$.
(Note that linear momentum is *not* conserved.)

In the collision, the angular frequency goes from $\omega_o$ to $0$.
Let $f$ be the average force of friction that acts horizontally on the ball during the collision.  Then from torque = $\Delta L/\Delta t$,
$fR = I\omega_o/\Delta t$
where $\Delta t$ is the collision time. (5)

Now apply $F = m\,\Delta v/\Delta t$ in the $x$-direction.
The $x$-component of velocity changes from $0$ to $v_x$ during time $\Delta t$, and the horizontal force is $f$:
$f = m\,v_x/\Delta t$. (5)

From the torque equation we have $f\Delta t = I\omega_o/R$, so combining the torque and force equations, (2)
$I\omega_o/R = m\,v_x$
and solving for $v_x$,
$v_x = I\omega_o / mR$ (2)

Now $v_x$ is known.  Thus, so is $v_y$.
$v_y = [\,2\beta K_1/m - v_x^2\,]^{1/2}$ (1)

problems.statement:
Consider the gravitational force $F$ on a planet due to the Sun when that force includes a small perturbation $\Gamma$ giving a departure from Newton's law of gravitation,

$$F = (1 + \Gamma)\,(GMm/R^2)$$

where $M$ is the Sun's mass, $m$ is the planet's mass, $G$ is Newton's constant, $R$ is the distance between the center of the Sun and the center of the planet, and we take $\Gamma$ to be a constant $\ll 1$.  (For example, general relativity provides such a perturbation.)  Approximate the orbit as circular.
problems.statementAfterParts:
Data:

Period of Mercury's orbit = 88 days

Radius of Mercury's orbit = $5.8\times10^{10}$ m

$G = 6.7\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{Nm^2/kg^2}$

Mass of Sun = $2.0\times10^{30}$ kg

$c = 3.0\times10^{8}$ m/s

3600" = 1 degree.

[This problem adapted from A.P. French, *Newtonian Mechanics*, Norton & Co., NY, 1971.]

parts.label: (a)
parts.statement: Show that the planet's period is $T \approx T_o(1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\Gamma)$, where $T_o$ would be the planet's period if there were no perturbation.

parts.label: (b)
parts.statement: In one revolution, a planet moving under the purely Newtonian force would travel through the angle $2\pi$.  But with the perturbation, in the same amount of time the planet travels through an additional angle $\delta$.  Calculate $\delta$ in terms of $\Gamma$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.statement: The general theory of relativity contributes the perturbation $\Gamma = 6v^2/c^2$ to Newton's law of gravitation, where $v$ is the speed of the planet relative to the Sun, and $c$ is the speed of light.  The precession angle $\delta$ of part (b) may be approximated as $\delta \approx (6\pi/c^2)(GM/R)$.  Demonstrate this claim that $\delta \approx (6\pi/c^2)(GM/R)$, by using your result of part (b) and the given perturbation.

parts.label: (d)
parts.statement: Using the result $\delta \approx (6\pi/c^2)(GM/R)$, and using the data below, calculate the numerical value of $\delta$ for the planet Mercury.  Express your answer in seconds of arc per century.  This is our simple model's prediction of general relativity's contribution to the precession of Mercury's orbit.

solution.statement:
**(a, 7)** From $F = ma$, since the orbit is circular so that the acceleration is $v^2/R$,
$(1 + \Gamma)\,(GMm/R^2) = mv^2/R$ (2)

Using  $v = 2\pi R/T$  where $T$ is the period, (2)

$F = ma$ becomes (after some re-arrangement)
$T^2 = (4\pi^2/GM)R^3\,(1 + \Gamma)^{-1}$
Notice that $T_o^2 = (4\pi^2/GM)R^3$, where $T_o$ is the period of the planet's orbit with purely the Newtonian force.  Hence,  $T = T_o(1 + \Gamma)^{-1/2}$ (2)

Since $\Gamma \ll 1$, by the binomial expansion
$T \approx T_o(1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\Gamma)$ (1)

**(b, 7)**
In elapsed time
$\Delta t = T_o$, the planet turns through the angle  $2\pi + \delta$ (2)

This angle can also be equated to $\omega T_o$ where $\omega$ is the planet's orbital angular velocity, viz.,
$\omega = 2\pi/T$
$\approx (2\pi/T_o)(1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\Gamma)^{-1}$ (2)

by virtue of the binomial expansion again,
$\omega \approx (2\pi/T_o)(1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\Gamma)$ (1)

Therefore, we complete the calculation:
$2\pi + \delta = \omega T_o$
$= (2\pi)(1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\Gamma)$
cancelling the $2\pi$,
$\delta = \pi\Gamma$. (2)

**(c, 2)**
$\delta = \pi\Gamma$
$= 6\pi v^2/c^2$
From $F = ma$ above, we may approximate $v^2$ with $GM/R$, (keeping the $\Gamma$ from $F = ma$ would give $\delta$ here to second order in $\Gamma$), so that
$\delta \approx 6\pi GM/Rc^2$ (2)

**(d, 4)**
For one lap around the Sun, from the given numerical data,
$\delta_1 = 6\pi GM/Rc^2$
$= 6\pi\,(6.7\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{Nm^2/kg^2})(2.0\times10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg})(3.0\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s})^{-2}(5.8\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m})^{-1}$
$= 4.8\times10^{-7}$ radians (2)

In 100 years, Mercury makes
$(365/88)\times100 \approx 415$ laps around the Sun. (1)

For 415 laps,
$\delta_{415} = 415\,(4.8\times10^{-7}$ radians$)$
$\approx 2\times10^{-4}$ radians
$= (2\times10^{-4})(180/\pi)$ degrees
$= (2\times10^{-4})(180/\pi)\,(3600'')$
$= 41''$. (1)
